subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Neutron Stars: City-Sized and Ultra-Dense
description: A fast breakdown of Neutron Stars: City-Sized and Ultra-Dense for builders.

hook.text: A neutron star is a collapsed stellar core just 20 km across—yet it weighs more than our Sun.

buildup.text: When a massive star's core collapses, protons and electrons merge into neutrons. The density is staggering.

discovery.text: A sugar-cube of neutron star material would weigh a billion tons on Earth.

twist.text: Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times per second, emitting beams of radiation like cosmic lighthouses.

climax.text: Jocelyn Bell discovered pulsars in 1967. Her supervisor won the Nobel Prize—she was controversially excluded.

punchline.text: A city-sized ball heavier than the Sun. Spinning hundreds of times per second.

quiz.question: How much would a sugar-cube of neutron star material weigh on Earth?

details.summary: Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars after supernova explosions — just 20 kilometers across but containing more mass than the Sun. Their density is so extreme that a teaspoon weighs a billion tons. Matter is compressed into neutrons, creating conditions found nowhere else.
details.whyItMatters: Neutron stars push physics to extremes. They're natural laboratories for testing matter under impossible conditions — densities, magnetic fields, and gravitational forces that no Earth experiment can replicate.
takeaways: Neutron stars are about 20 km across with more mass than the Sun
A teaspoon of neutron star weighs roughly a billion tons
They test physics under conditions unreplicable on Earth

faq.question: What happens to matter inside a neutron star?
faq.answer: Under extreme pressure, electrons are forced into protons, creating neutrons (and neutrinos). The entire star becomes essentially a giant atomic nucleus. Near the core, matter may form exotic states — quark soup, superfluid neutrons, or other phases unknown to terrestrial physics.

faq.question: How fast do neutron stars spin?
faq.answer: Conservation of angular momentum from the original star's rotation accelerates to extreme rates during collapse. Newly formed neutron stars can spin hundreds of times per second. The fastest known pulsar rotates 716 times per second — its equator moves at 24% of light speed.
